app.title: TESS Target Pixels Inspector
app.summary: A person enters a target ID, with an optional observing sector and magnitude limit, and the app downloads that target's pixel data. A sky view shows the pixels with catalog sources drawn on top. The person can switch catalogs on and off, search for a source by ID, and click a source to read its details and links. Next they build a light curve from pixels they select, step through the frames in time, and draw one small light curve for each pixel over the zoomed time and pixel range. Last, they paste a link to an external survey light curve and fold it by a period, to check which nearby source the variable signal comes from.

task.text: Find which star among the sources near a target is producing a variable signal, by checking the signal pixel by pixel against catalog positions and other surveys' light curves.

data.text: A stack of image frames over time from one patch of sky, light curves built from those pixels, catalog tables of nearby sources with positions and magnitudes, and light curves from other surveys fetched by URL
data.item: a pixel in a time-stacked image cutout around one target, with the catalog sources that fall on it

stage.text: vetting where a detected variable signal comes from, before claiming or following up the source

mechanism.text: A pixel image with catalog sources overlaid acts as the spatial overview. Clicking a source opens its details, and selecting pixels rebuilds the light curve next to the image. The cadence slider and clicks on the light curve keep the image frame and the time marker in step. A per-pixel grid and an external light curve viewer, which can fold by period, give closer and independent views of the same signal.

field.text: pixel-level photometry and source identification for variable signals in time-domain astronomy

workflow.name: trace a signal back to its source among nearby objects

steps.here: A plain HTML form takes a target ID (TIC), plus an optional sector and magnitude limit. On Show the app searches the archive and downloads the pixel file (SPOC or TessCut), showing an in-progress message while it works.

steps.step: look over every item at a glance
steps.here: The sky view draws the pixel image a few days into the sector. It marks the target with a cross and overlays sources from Gaia DR3/TIC, ZTF, ASAS-SN SkyPatrol and VSX, each corrected for proper motion and sized by magnitude. Checkboxes show or hide each catalog, and a stretch slider adjusts the image.

Typing a Gaia DR3 source, TIC or other ID selects that star among the visible catalogs. Clicking a star does the same. Either way an arrow points to the star and a table lists its magnitudes, separation and links to catalog pages and variability cross-matches.

steps.step: compute a value from the data
steps.here: Inspect builds a light curve from the pipeline aperture, or from the target's own pixel in TessCut data. Clicking or shift-clicking pixels rebuilds it straight away. Options set normalization, rough background subtraction and manual y limits.

steps.step: step through items one at a time
steps.here: A cadence slider and < / > buttons move through the image frames while a vertical marker follows on the light curve. Clicking a point on the light curve jumps the image to that frame.
Per-Pixel Plot draws a grid with one small light curve per pixel. It covers only the pixel and time range currently zoomed, with the selected aperture outlined, and warns when the time span is long.

Pasting a ZTF CSV or SkyPatrol v2 URL plots that survey's light curve in magnitudes. A period and epoch (BTJD or HJD) fold it, 1/2 P and 2x P re-fold at half or double the period, and a color map can show time within the phase plot.

distinctive: Catalog positions are corrected for proper motion to the observation date, so sources line up with where they actually were on the pixels
Several independent catalogs and surveys are overlaid on the same pixels, and the last-drawn layer gets priority when an ID is searched
Clicking pixels rebuilds the aperture light curve live, so the person can see which pixels the signal sits in
Per-pixel light curves are limited to the zoomed region and time window, to keep them readable
An external survey light curve can be folded and the period halved or doubled, to check whether a neighbor shows the same periodic signal
